title: Animals with a backbone: the five groups and how they keep warm

summary.text: A house lizard and a pigeon both have a backbone, but they keep warm in very different ways. Animals with a backbone are called vertebrates, and scientists sort them into five groups: fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals. Birds and mammals make their own body heat from food. Most fish, amphibians and reptiles take their warmth from the sun, the ground or the water around them. The groups also differ in how they breathe and how they have babies, and scientists still argue about how warm the dinosaurs were.
summary.art: Five animals a city child can meet, in a row: a fish on ice at the market, a frog by a monsoon puddle, a house lizard on a wall, a puffed-up pigeon on a window ledge, and a dog lying in the shade, each with a small sun or flame symbol above them.

intro.hook: In a cold north Indian winter, the house lizards in many homes seem to disappear for weeks. The pigeons on the window ledge stay busy all winter. Where do the lizards go, and why don't the pigeons need to hide?
intro.text: The house lizard and the pigeon both have a backbone. Both breathe air. But they keep warm in two different ways. A lizard's body is about as warm as the air around them. On cold days they hide in a crack or behind a cupboard, still and slow, until the weather warms up. A pigeon makes heat inside their own body from the food they eat, all day and all night. Where winters are warm, as in Chennai or Kochi, house lizards stay active all year, because the air never gets cold enough to slow them. You will meet five groups of animals with a backbone, and find out how each one breathes, stays warm or cool, and has their babies.
intro.art: A flat's window in winter: outside, two puffed-up pigeons on the ledge; inside, a house lizard tucked still behind a picture frame on the wall.

outcomes: I can name the five groups of animals with a backbone, and give two Indian examples of each.
I can say how each group breathes: gills for fish, gills then lungs and skin for most amphibians, and lungs for reptiles, birds and mammals.
I can explain the difference between animals that make their own body heat (birds and mammals) and animals that take their heat from outside (most fish, amphibians and reptiles).
I can describe how animals keep warm with fur, feathers and fat, and keep cool with shade, mud, panting and sweat.
I can say how each group has young: jelly eggs in water, shelled eggs on land, or babies born alive and fed on milk.
I can run a fair test with a thermometer, record the numbers in a table, and say what I think, what I saw and why.
I can say what scientists agree on about body heat, and what they still argue about, like warm-bodied dinosaurs and the very first warm animals.

terms.meaning: An animal with a backbone. A backbone is a chain of small bones down the middle of the back.
terms.example: A cow, a crow, a cobra, a frog and a rohu fish are all vertebrates.
terms.art: Five animal outlines, each with their backbone drawn as a glowing chain of beads.

terms.meaning: The chain of small bones that runs down the back. It holds the body up and protects the spinal cord, the thick nerve inside it.
terms.example: Run your fingers down the middle of your back. The bumps you feel are your backbone.
terms.art: A child's back with a soft glow showing the bumpy line of the backbone.

terms.meaning: Vertebrates that live in water, breathe with gills and usually have fins and scales.
terms.example: Rohu, katla, the mahseer of mountain rivers, and the shark are all fish.
terms.art: A rohu fish swimming, with their fins and shining scales labelled by pictures, not words.

terms.meaning: Vertebrates that usually start life in water and later live on land too. They have soft, damp skin with no scales.
terms.example: Frogs, toads and the legless caecilians of the Western Ghats are amphibians.
terms.art: A frog half in a pond and half on a wet leaf, their skin shiny and damp.

terms.meaning: Vertebrates with dry, scaly skin that breathe with lungs. Most lay eggs with leathery shells on land.
terms.example: Lizards, snakes, turtles, tortoises and crocodiles are reptiles.
terms.art: A mugger crocodile, a cobra and a star tortoise side by side, their scales clear.

terms.meaning: Vertebrates with feathers, a beak and wings. All birds lay eggs with hard shells.
terms.example: Sparrows, peacocks, ostriches and penguins are birds, even the ones that cannot fly.
terms.art: A peacock, a house sparrow and a penguin standing together, feathers fluffed.

terms.meaning: Vertebrates with hair or fur. Mammal mothers feed their babies on milk.
terms.example: Cows, cats, bats, elephants, dolphins and people are mammals.
terms.art: A cow feeding her calf, a bat hanging, and a dolphin jumping, all with soft fur or skin.

terms.meaning: Thin, red, frilly parts on each side of a fish's head, under a hard flap. They take oxygen out of water.
terms.example: Look at a fresh fish at the market. Lift the hard flap behind their eye. The red frills are gills.
terms.art: A fish head with the gill cover lifted, showing bright red feathery gills and water flowing past.

terms.meaning: Two soft, spongy organs inside the chest that take oxygen out of air.
terms.example: When you breathe in deeply, your chest gets bigger because your lungs fill with air.
terms.art: A child breathing in, with two pink balloon-like lungs glowing inside the chest.

terms.meaning: A gas in air and water that every animal needs. Our bodies use it to get energy out of food.
terms.example: You breathe in oxygen all the time, even while you sleep.
terms.art: Tiny blue dots of oxygen floating in air above a pond and in the water below it.

terms.meaning: The warmth inside a body. It comes from food being used up in the body, or from the sun and the air around it.
terms.example: Your cheeks feel warm when you touch them, even in the shade.
terms.art: A child holding a hand to their own warm cheek, soft orange glow around the face.

terms.meaning: An animal whose body makes their own heat from food, so they stay warm even when the air is cold. Scientists call them an endotherm.
terms.example: A sparrow, a dog and you all make your own heat. That is why your body stays near 37 degrees.
terms.art: A small bird on a frosty wire with a tiny glowing stove drawn inside their chest.

terms.meaning: An animal that gets most of their warmth from the sun, warm ground or warm water around them. Scientists call them an ectotherm.
terms.example: A lizard lies on a sunny wall in the morning to warm up before they hunt.
terms.art: A lizard stretched on a sunny stone with sunbeams pouring onto their back.

terms.meaning: Old words for 'takes heat from outside' and 'makes their own heat'. They can mislead, because a lizard in the sun can have warmer blood than you.
terms.example: A lizard on a hot rock in May can be warmer than a person in the shade.
terms.art: A thermometer beside a sunbathing lizard reading higher than one beside a child in the shade.

terms.meaning: A tool that measures how hot or cold something is. It shows the answer in degrees Celsius, written °C.
terms.example: A doctor's thermometer under your tongue shows about 37 °C when you are well.
terms.art: A digital thermometer showing 37.0 next to a glass thermometer with a red line.

terms.meaning: Something that slows heat from moving in or out. Fur, feathers, fat and wool are insulation.
terms.example: A woollen sweater keeps your warmth in on a winter morning.
terms.art: A puffed-up pigeon, a woolly sheep and a child in a sweater, with little heat arrows kept inside.

terms.meaning: Lying in the sun to soak up its warmth.
terms.example: Mugger crocodiles bask on riverbanks with their mouths open.
terms.art: A mugger crocodile on a sandy riverbank in the sun, mouth open.

terms.meaning: Breathing fast with the mouth open to cool down. Water dries off the tongue and carries heat away.
terms.example: A dog pants on a hot afternoon, with their tongue hanging out.
terms.art: A street dog panting in the shade of an auto, tongue out.

terms.meaning: A package in which a baby animal grows before they hatch. It holds food, water and the growing baby.
terms.example: A hen's egg, a frog's jelly egg and a turtle's leathery egg are all eggs.
terms.art: Three eggs in a row: frogspawn in water, a soft turtle egg in sand, and a hen's egg in straw.

terms.meaning: An egg with a hard or leathery cover that keeps it from drying out, so it can be laid on land.
terms.example: Birds and most reptiles lay shelled eggs. The shell has thousands of tiny holes that let air in.
terms.art: A hen's egg with a magnifying circle showing tiny holes in the shell and air passing through.

terms.meaning: The food a mammal mother makes in her body to feed her babies.
terms.example: A goat kid drinks their mother's milk. A human baby does too.
terms.art: A goat feeding her kid in a village courtyard.

explanations.definition: Vertebrates are animals with a backbone. Scientists usually sort them into five big groups: fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals.
explanations.description: Every vertebrate has a backbone inside their body, made of many small bones. The five groups are told apart by their skin, how they breathe, how they keep warm and how they have young. Fish have scales and fins and live in water. Amphibians have soft, damp skin. Reptiles have dry scales. Birds have feathers. Mammals have hair and feed their babies milk. Only a small share of all animals have a backbone. Most animals, like insects and worms, do not.
examples: A rohu fish has scales, fins and gills.
A frog has damp skin with no scales.
A cobra has dry scales.
A crow has feathers.
A goat has hair and feeds her kid milk.
explanations.art: Five cards in a row, each with one animal and a close-up of their skin: scales, damp skin, dry scales, feathers and fur.
explanations.context: This card names the five groups of animals with a backbone. The rest of the unit compares them.

explanations.definition: Fish breathe with gills. Gills take oxygen out of water.
explanations.description: Water has a little oxygen mixed into it. You cannot see it, just as you cannot see sugar mixed into tea. A fish gulps water through their mouth. The water flows over their gills and out under the hard flap behind their head. The gills are thin, red and frilly. Blood inside them picks up the oxygen from the water. Water holds much less oxygen than air, about thirty times less. So a fish must keep water flowing over their gills all the time. Out of water, the frills stick together and stop working. That is why most fish die quickly on land.
examples: A goldfish in a bowl opens and shuts their mouth, and the flaps behind their eyes move too. They are pumping water over their gills.
A shark swims with their mouth a little open, so water rushes over their gills.
Fish in a warm, crowded pond come up to gulp at the top when the water runs low on oxygen.
explanations.art: A cut-away fish with arrows of water going in at the mouth, over red feathery gills and out at the side, tiny oxygen dots moving into the blood.
explanations.context: This card explains how fish breathe under water. The next card compares the other four groups.

explanations.concept: How amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals breathe
explanations.definition: Reptiles, birds and mammals breathe air with lungs. Most amphibians breathe with gills when young, then with lungs and their damp skin when grown.
explanations.description: A tadpole lives in water and breathes with gills, like a fish. As they grow into a frog, they grow lungs. A frog also breathes through their thin, wet skin. That is why frogs must stay damp. If their skin dries, they cannot breathe well. Reptiles have dry skin, so they breathe only with lungs. Birds have lungs plus extra air bags, called air sacs, that push air through the lungs in one direction. This gives them lots of oxygen for flying. Mammals breathe with lungs too. Even whales and dolphins, which live in water, must come up to breathe air.
examples: A frog's throat pumps up and down as they push air into their lungs.
A Ganges river dolphin, India's national aquatic animal, comes up for air every minute or two.
A bar-headed goose can fly over the Himalayas, where the air is very thin, because their lungs and air sacs work so well.
explanations.art: Four small pictures: a tadpole with gills, a frog with lungs and shiny skin, a lizard with lungs, and a bird with lungs and balloon-like air sacs.
explanations.context: This card explains how the four groups that are not fish breathe. Breathing is covered in more detail in the unit on animal bodies.

explanations.definition: Birds and mammals make their own body heat from food. Most fish, amphibians and reptiles take their heat from the sun, the ground or the water around them.
explanations.description: Your body is like a little stove. It burns food, slowly and without flames, and that makes heat. Birds and mammals do this all the time. So they stay warm on a cold night, and can move fast even on a winter morning. Scientists call them endotherms, which means 'heat from inside'. Most fish, amphibians and reptiles make only a little heat. Their bodies warm up and cool down with the world around them. Scientists call them ectotherms, which means 'heat from outside'. A lizard is slow on a cold morning. They lie in the sun to warm up first. Then they can run and hunt.
examples: You stay near 37 °C on a cold night and on a hot day.
A sparrow keeps their body at about 40 °C, even on a frosty morning in Ooty.
A garden lizard basks on a wall in the morning sun, then runs fast once they are warm.
A frog in a cold pond moves slowly, because their body is as cold as the water.
explanations.art: Two thermometers through the day: one beside a dog that stays level, one beside a lizard that goes up and down with the sun.
explanations.context: This card is about the two ways animals keep warm. It is the main idea of the unit.

explanations.definition: Animals that take their heat from outside are not always cold. Their bodies warm up and cool down with the sun, the ground and the air around them.
explanations.description: People used to call lizards, snakes and fish 'cold-blooded'. But a lizard basking on a sunny wall in May can be warmer than you. Their blood is not cold at all. What is different is where the heat comes from. The lizard takes their heat from the sun. You make it from food. So scientists prefer the words 'takes heat from outside' and 'makes their own heat'. Even this is not a perfect split. Some big fish, like tuna, keep their muscles warm. A fish called the opah keeps their whole body a little warmer than the sea.
examples: A desert lizard's body can reach about 40 °C on a hot afternoon.
A tuna's swimming muscles stay warmer than the cold water they swim in.
A python mother coils around her eggs and shivers her muscles to keep them warm.
explanations.art: A smiling lizard on a hot rock holding a thermometer showing 40, beside a puzzled child in the shade whose thermometer shows 37.
explanations.context: This card explains why the old word 'cold-blooded' does not really fit.

explanations.concept: Keeping warm: fur, feathers, fat and huddling
explanations.definition: Fur, feathers and fat slow heat from leaking out of a body. Scientists call this insulation.
explanations.description: Making heat uses lots of food. So animals that make their own heat try not to waste it. Fur and feathers trap a thin layer of still air next to the skin. Still air lets heat pass very slowly. That is why a pigeon puffs up their feathers on a cold morning. They are making a thicker coat of trapped air. Whales and seals have a thick layer of fat under the skin, called blubber. Penguins huddle in a tight crowd, so less of each body touches the icy wind. Shivering helps too. Shaking muscles make extra heat.
examples: A house sparrow on a winter morning looks round and fat. They have fluffed up their feathers.
A yak in Ladakh has long, thick hair that keeps them warm at minus 30 °C.
A litter of puppies sleeps in a heap to share warmth.
You shiver when you climb out of a cold pool. Your muscles are making heat.
explanations.art: A puffed-up pigeon with a magnified circle showing tiny pockets of air trapped between their feathers.
explanations.context: This card explains how animals that make their own heat stop it from leaking away.

explanations.concept: Keeping cool: shade, mud, panting and sweat
explanations.definition: Animals cool down by finding shade, by wetting their bodies, or by letting water dry off them. Drying water carries heat away.
explanations.description: When water dries off your skin, it takes heat with it. That is why a wet cloth on your forehead feels cool. People sweat, and the sweat dries and cools the skin. Dogs have very few sweat glands, so they pant. Water dries off their tongue and mouth. Buffaloes cannot sweat much, so they lie in mud or water. Elephants flap their huge ears. The ears are thin and full of blood vessels, and the moving air cools the blood. Animals that take their heat from outside cool down simply by moving into shade, into water or under the ground.
examples: A buffalo lies in a muddy pond on a hot afternoon.
An elephant flaps their ears in the summer heat.
A street dog pants under a parked car.
A lizard leaves the hot wall at noon and hides in a crack.
explanations.art: Four pictures: a buffalo wallowing, an elephant flapping their ears, a dog panting, a lizard slipping into a wall crack.
explanations.context: This card explains how animals stay cool when it is hot.

explanations.concept: Why making your own heat costs lots of food
explanations.definition: Animals that make their own heat need many times more food than animals of the same size that take heat from outside.
explanations.description: A stove needs fuel all the time. So does a warm body. A mouse needs to eat every day. A snake of the same weight can go for weeks without eating. Scientists have measured this. An animal that makes their own heat uses roughly five to ten times as much energy at rest. In return, they can stay active at night, in winter and in cold places. Animals that take their heat from outside save food. But they are slow when it is cold, and they must wait for the sun.
examples: A tiny sunbird visits flowers all day long, because they burn food so fast.
A python can eat one big meal and then rest for weeks.
In cold winters, some frogs and turtles stay still, buried in mud, and hardly use any food.
explanations.art: A see-saw with a pile of food on one side and a small mouse, and a single small meal on the other side with a big, sleeping python.
explanations.context: This card explains the cost of making your own body heat.

explanations.definition: Fish and amphibians usually lay soft eggs in water. Reptiles and birds lay shelled eggs on land. Most mammals give birth to live babies and feed them milk.
explanations.description: A fish or frog egg has no shell. It is soft and wrapped in jelly. In air it would dry out, so it must be laid in water. Reptiles and birds lay eggs with a shell. The shell keeps water in but lets air pass through thousands of tiny holes. So these eggs can be laid on dry land. Bird eggs must be kept warm, so birds sit on them. Most reptiles bury their eggs in warm sand or leaves. Most mammals grow their babies inside the mother's body, then feed them milk. There are exceptions. Some sharks and some snakes give birth to live young. Two kinds of mammals, the platypus and the echidna, lay eggs.
examples: A frog lays a floating clump of jelly eggs in a monsoon puddle.
An olive ridley turtle digs a hole on an Odisha beach and lays about a hundred eggs.
A hen sits on her eggs for about three weeks.
A cow gives birth to a calf, and the calf drinks her milk within an hour.
explanations.art: Three panels: frogspawn in a puddle, a turtle laying eggs in sand at night, a calf drinking from their mother.
explanations.context: This card compares how the five groups have babies.

explanations.definition: Animals that lay many eggs usually leave them. Animals that have only a few young usually care for them.
explanations.description: A rohu fish can lay lakhs of eggs and swims away. Most of the babies are eaten, but a few survive. A bird lays a few eggs and keeps them warm. Then they feed the chicks for days or weeks. Mammals have the fewest babies and look after them longest. An elephant calf stays close to their mother for years. There are surprises in every group. A mugger crocodile mother guards her nest and carries her hatchlings to the water in her mouth. A male emperor penguin holds the egg on his feet for about two months in the Antarctic winter. A female great hornbill seals herself inside a tree hole with her eggs, and the male feeds her through a slit.
examples: A rohu leaves her eggs in the river.
A king cobra mother builds a nest of leaves and guards her eggs.
Both pigeon parents feed their chicks a soft food made in their throats, called crop milk.
A langur baby clings to their mother's belly all day.
explanations.art: A mugger crocodile gently carrying tiny hatchlings in her open mouth towards a river.
explanations.context: This card is about how much each kind of animal looks after their babies.

explanations.concept: Temperature can decide boy or girl
explanations.definition: In many turtles and in crocodiles, the warmth of the nest decides whether a baby becomes male or female.
explanations.description: In birds and mammals, a baby is a boy or a girl from the very start. But in many reptiles, the sand around the egg decides. In olive ridley sea turtles, warmer nests give more females. Cooler nests give more males. This is one more way the sun and the ground shape the life of an animal that takes their heat from outside. It also means a warmer world could change how many male and female turtles hatch. Scientists are studying this on beaches around the world.
examples: Olive ridley nests on Rushikulya beach in Odisha are studied by forest staff and scientists.
Crocodile breeders can predict whether babies will be male or female from how warm the eggs were kept.
explanations.art: A turtle nest cut in half, the warm sun-side eggs coloured one shade and the cool deep eggs another.
explanations.context: This card is about a surprising way warmth shapes reptile babies.

explanations.concept: Where body heat really comes from: atoms and the sun
explanations.definition: Heat is the jiggling of tiny particles, such as atoms. A warm body has fast-jiggling atoms. Nearly all the warmth of animals comes, in the end, from the sun.
explanations.description: Everything is made of atoms, far too tiny to see. When something is warm, its atoms jiggle faster. A lizard on a sunny wall is warmed directly. Sunlight makes the atoms in their skin jiggle. A bird or a mammal is warmed another way. They eat food. Inside their cells, tiny parts called mitochondria break the food down slowly, and some of the energy comes out as heat. But that food's energy came from plants. And plants caught it from sunlight. So the lizard takes their warmth from the sun quickly, and the sparrow takes the sun's warmth slowly, through food. The sunlight left the sun about eight minutes before it reached the Earth.
examples: A lizard on a wall is warmed by sunlight that left the sun about eight minutes earlier.
Your breakfast idli came from rice, which grew using sunlight.
Newborn babies have a special 'brown fat' that makes extra heat to keep them warm.
explanations.art: A long path of light from the sun splitting in two: one ray straight onto a basking lizard, the other into a rice field, an idli and then a warm child.
explanations.context: This card follows body heat all the way back to atoms and the sun.

explanations.concept: When did animals first make their own heat?
explanations.description: Scientists agree that birds and mammals both make their own heat. Most think the two groups began to make their own heat separately, long ago. But nobody is sure exactly when, or why, it started. And they argue about dinosaurs. Birds came from dinosaurs, so maybe some dinosaurs were warm too. The main ideas are below.
examples: Fossils of some dinosaurs show feathers, which could have kept them warm.
Growth rings in dinosaur bones show how fast they grew, a clue to how warm they were.

perspectives.who: Many scientists who study fossils of feathered dinosaurs
perspectives.explanation: Some dinosaurs had feathers and grew fast, like birds. So they probably made their own heat, at least partly.
From the growth of dinosaur bones, they suggested dinosaurs were in between. They made some heat, but less than birds or mammals.

perspectives.who: Scientists who study very large animals
perspectives.explanation: Giant dinosaurs were so big they would stay warm just from their size, like a big pot of water that cools slowly. So they did not need to make much heat.

explanations.art: Three dinosaurs in a row: one cold and sluggish, one middle-warm, one fluffy and warm like a bird, each with a question mark.
explanations.context: This card is about a question scientists still argue about: when did warm bodies begin, and were dinosaurs warm?

agreed.text: Vertebrates are sorted into five big groups: fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals.
agreed.evidence: These groups share body plans, ways of breathing and ways of having young. Fossils and DNA both show they are related, branching from early fish.

agreed.text: Fish breathe with gills, and reptiles, birds and mammals breathe with lungs.
agreed.evidence: We can see gills and lungs when we look inside these animals, and we can measure the oxygen they take in.

agreed.text: Birds and mammals make their own body heat. Most fish, amphibians and reptiles take heat from outside.
agreed.evidence: Thermometers show that a bird's or mammal's body stays at the same warmth all day. A lizard's warmth goes up and down with the sun.

agreed.text: Shelled eggs let reptiles and birds lay eggs on dry land.
agreed.evidence: Shelled eggs keep their water in air, while frog and fish eggs dry up. The oldest shelled-egg animals appear in rocks more than 300 million years old.

agreed.text: Making your own heat uses much more food.
agreed.evidence: Scientists have measured the oxygen and food used by mice and lizards of the same weight. The mouse uses many times more.

challenging.who: Many people, because of the old word 'cold-blooded'.
challenging.for: Frogs and fish feel cool to touch, and lizards are slow on cold mornings.
challenging.against: A lizard basking in the sun can be warmer than a person. Their body warms and cools with their surroundings, so they are not always cold.
challenging.context: This card is about a common mistake caused by an old word.

challenging.claim: Animals that make their own heat are more advanced than the others.
challenging.who: An old view of nature as a ladder, with mammals and humans at the top.
challenging.for: Birds and mammals can stay active in cold places and at night.
challenging.against: Reptiles, fish and amphibians are just as well suited to their own lives. They need far less food. Evolution is a branching tree, not a ladder.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that some animal groups are better than others.

challenging.claim: The five groups are the natural, final way to sort vertebrates.
challenging.for: The five groups are easy to see and very useful.
challenging.against: Scientists who sort by family trees point out that birds are a branch of the reptiles. Birds are closer cousins of crocodiles than lizards are. The groups are a helpful choice, not a law of nature.
challenging.context: This card asks whether the five groups are the only right way to sort vertebrates.

challenging.for: Bird lungs with their air sacs are very special, and air flows through them in one direction.
challenging.against: In 2010, C.G. Farmer and Kent Sanders showed that air also flows one way through the lungs of alligators. This may be a very old trick, shared by birds and crocodiles.
challenging.context: This card is about a surprise discovery in crocodile lungs.

big_questions.q: Why do you think frogs need water to lay eggs, but crocodiles do not?
big_questions.hint: What happens to a jelly sweet left out in the sun?

big_questions.q: If your body is a little stove, what is its fuel? And where did the fuel's energy come from?
big_questions.hint: Follow your lunch back to the field and the sky.

big_questions.q: Is it better to make your own heat, or to take it from the sun? Can one way be better for everyone?
big_questions.hint: Think about food, cold nights and hot deserts.

big_questions.q: A mugger mother carries her babies in her mouth. A rohu fish leaves her eggs. Is one a better parent?
big_questions.hint: Think about how many babies each one has.

big_questions.q: Your body keeps making heat, and the heat keeps leaving you. Where does your warmth go?
big_questions.hint: Think of the warm chair after you stand up, and the bottle in the dry sock.

big_questions.q: Why do you think a tiny bird needs to eat all day, but a big snake can wait for weeks?
big_questions.hint: Think of a small pot and a big pot of hot water. Which cools faster?

story.title: Two Kinds of Warm
story.note: The village of Napasar is a real place near Bikaner in Rajasthan. Noor, her Dadi and everything that happens are made up. The facts are real: garden lizards are slow and darker in colour until the sun warms them, sparrow chicks are born almost bare and must be kept warm by a parent, and a quilt or feathers only hold heat in.
text: In the desert village of Napasar, winter mornings are sharp and cold. The sand is cold under bare feet. The water in the matka is so cold it hurts your teeth. Noor, who was nine, ran out into the courtyard with her shawl trailing behind her.

She stopped. On the flat stone by the neem tree lay a garden lizard. Their skin had gone a dull, dark grey. Their legs were stuck out sideways like twigs. Noor crouched down. She waved her hand above them. They did not blink.
"Dadi," she called. "The girgit is dead."
Her grandmother came out slowly, holding a steel tumbler of tea in both hands for warmth. She looked at the lizard for a long time. Then she sipped her tea.
"They are not dead," said Dadi. "They are waiting."
"Waiting for what?"
Dadi pointed at the wall. A line of yellow light was creeping down it, brick by brick. "For that," she said.

Noor did not believe her. But she sat on the step and watched. The light slid down the wall. It reached the edge of the stone. It touched the lizard's tail, then their back, then their head. For a long time nothing happened. Noor's toes were freezing. Then one eye opened. Then the other. Their dark skin slowly turned paler and brighter. The lizard lifted themself up on their front legs, like an old man getting out of a chair. Then, all at once, they were gone. A flick of tail, and they were up the neem tree.
Noor laughed out loud. "They came back to life!"
"They were never gone," said Dadi. "The girgit has no fire inside. They take their warmth from the sun. At night they go cold and slow, and in the morning they take back the warmth. Every day."
Noor thought about that all morning. At school she told her friend Bhanwar, who said lizards were boring. Noor did not think they were boring at all.

In the afternoon, a strong wind blew dust through the village. When Noor came home, she heard a thin cheeping from the corner of the courtyard. A baby sparrow lay on the ground under the roof beams. Their nest of straw and string was up in a gap in the beams, too high to reach. The chick was almost bare. They had only a few grey tufts and a big yellow mouth. They were shaking.

Noor knew what to do. She had learned it that very morning. She carried the chick carefully to the flat stone by the neem tree, where the sun was still shining, and laid them down. "Wait for the sun," she whispered to them, in Dadi's voice.
She sat on the step to watch them come back to life.

But this time something was wrong. The chick did not get stronger. They shook harder. The sun on the stone was weak and low now, and it was sliding away up the wall, the opposite way from the morning. In a few minutes the stone would be in shadow. And then the long, freezing night would come.
"Dadi!"
Dadi came out with a lantern, though it was not dark yet. She looked at the chick. She looked at the sun going away. Then she looked at Noor.

"The girgit can wait all night in the cold," she said. "They go slow and still, and the cold does not harm them. But this little one is different. They have a fire inside. A tiny one. It must keep burning all night, or it goes out."
"Then they need more sun!"
"Look, the sun is leaving. What else keeps a fire from going out?"

Noor looked at the lantern. The flame was inside a glass, safe from the wind. She looked at her own shawl. She thought of how warm she stayed under her quilt at night, even when the room was icy. The quilt did not make any heat. It just held hers in.

She knelt and scooped the chick up into her two cupped hands. They were so light it felt like holding a leaf. She held them against her chest and pulled her woollen shawl over her hands. She could feel the chick's heart going very fast, like rain on a tin roof. Slowly, slowly, the shaking stopped.
"Your hands are warm," said Dadi softly. "Your hands are a fire too."

They waited for Noor's mother to come home. She climbed the ladder with the chick in a soft cloth and slid them back into the nest. At once there was a flutter. The mother sparrow had been on the roof all along, chirping angrily. Now she dived into the gap. Noor saw her spread her feathers wide and settle down over her babies, round and puffed up, like a warm brown cushion.

That night Noor lay under her quilt and thought about the two kinds of warm. The lizard, cold all night, waiting for the sun to come back. The chick, burning their own tiny fire, safe under their mother's feathers.
"Dadi," she whispered across the dark room. "Where does the sparrow's fire come from?"
"From the grain she eats," said Dadi sleepily.
"And where does the grain get it?"
Dadi was quiet for so long that Noor thought she was asleep. Then she said, "The bajra grows in the fields all summer, Noor. What do they drink all day, besides water?"
Noor thought of the long summer days, the bajra plants standing in the blazing light, and she smiled into the dark.

In the morning, the girgit was on their stone, grey and still, waiting. Noor did not call anyone this time. She sat down next to them with her hands under her shawl, and they waited for the sun together.
story.epiphany: For the parent: the lizard and the chick are both cold, but they need different help. The lizard takes their heat from outside, so the sun is all they need, and a cold night only makes them slow. The chick makes their own heat from food, but they are tiny and almost bare, so their heat leaks away fast. More sun cannot help once the sun is setting. What they need is insulation, something to hold their own heat in, and a warm body beside it. That is why birds sit on their chicks. The last turn follows the warmth back to its source. The sparrow's heat comes from grain, and the grain's energy came from sunlight. Both kinds of warm are the sun's warmth, taken by two different paths.
ask: Why did Noor think the lizard was dead? What was really happening?
Why did the sun help the lizard but not the chick?
Noor's quilt makes no heat. So how does it keep her warm?
What did the mother sparrow do when the chick came back? Why?
Dadi asked what the bajra drinks all day. What do you think she meant?

printables.title: 5 question cards
items: BREATHE: How does this animal breathe?
WARM: Do they make their own heat, or take heat from outside?
COOL: How do they cool down on a hot day?
YOUNG: Do they lay jelly eggs, shelled eggs, or give birth?
CARE: Do they look after their babies? How?

printables.title: Five family mats
items: FISH: gills, fins, eggs in water
BIRDS: feathers, hard eggs, make heat

rules: Cut out the 25 animal cards and the 5 question cards. Lay out the five family mats.
Shuffle the animal cards and deal 5 to each player. Put the rest face down in a pile.
Shuffle the question cards and put them face down in their own pile. When they run out, shuffle them and use them again.
On your turn, take the top animal card from the pile (if the pile is empty, skip this). Then turn over the top question card.
Choose any animal in your hand and answer the question for that animal. Then say which family mat it belongs on. The mats list the clues to check against.
If the others agree, put the animal on the right mat and score one point.
If you are wrong, the others tell you the right answer. The card still goes on the right mat, but with no point. The next player goes.
The player who puts the last card on a mat gets a bonus point.
When all 25 cards are on the mats, the player with the most points wins. A tie is a shared win.
