flow.do: 1. Cut out the cards and lay out the five family mats in a row. 2. Shuffle and deal 5 animal cards to each player. 3. Put the question cards in a pile, face down.
flow.say: Every animal on these cards has a backbone. They belong to five families: fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals. To put an animal on their family mat, you must answer a question about them.
flow.kid: Lay out the five mats: fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals. Get five animal cards. To place a card, answer a question about it.
flow.context: This is the first step of Five Families, a card game about animals with backbones. Here you set up the game.

flow.do: Play a practice round together with the Rohu fish card and the BREATHE question.
flow.say: Let's practise. Here is the rohu, the fish you see at the market. How does a rohu breathe?
flow.kid: Practice card: the rohu fish. How do they breathe? Say your answer.
flow.context: This is a practice round of Five Families. The animal is a rohu fish, and the question is how they breathe.

good: With gills.
They take water through their mouth and over their gills.

check.q: How does a rohu fish breathe?
options: With lungs, like us
With gills, which take oxygen out of water
Through their scales
check.why: Fish breathe with gills. Water flows in at the mouth, over the red frills, and out at the sides. Picking lungs usually means thinking all animals breathe the way we do. Picking scales mixes up a fish with a frog, which breathes partly through their skin.

flow.do: Play the WARM question with the Garden lizard card.
flow.say: Here is a garden lizard. Do they make their own heat, or take heat from outside? Remember the lizard on the wall in the morning.
flow.kid: Game moment: the garden lizard. Where does their warmth come from?
flow.context: This is a game moment in Five Families. The question is where a garden lizard gets their warmth.

check.q: Where does a garden lizard get their warmth?
options: They make their own heat from food, like us
They take heat from outside, from the sun and warm stones
They have no warmth at all
check.why: Lizards are reptiles. Most reptiles take their heat from outside. That is why they bask in the morning sun. Picking 'no warmth' usually comes from the old word 'cold-blooded'. A lizard in the sun can be warmer than you.

flow.do: Play the game until all 25 cards are on the mats. Keep score on the score sheet.
flow.say: Now let's play properly. Take turns. If you are not sure, think about the animal's skin first. Is it scaly, damp, feathery or furry?
flow.kid: Now play the game. Take turns with the cards. Not sure? Look at the skin. Scales, damp skin, feathers or fur?
flow.context: This is the main part of Five Families. Players answer questions and place animals on their family mats.
flow.parent: Tricky cards: the purple frog and the caecilian are amphibians. The caecilian looks like a big worm, but they have a backbone. The bat and the dolphin are mammals. The penguin and ostrich are birds, even though they cannot fly. The seahorse is a fish.

flow.do: Pick up the bat card and ask the question below.
flow.say: Let's look at a tricky one. A bat flies, like a bird. Why are they a mammal?
flow.kid: Game moment: the bat. They fly. Are they a bird or a mammal?
flow.context: This is a game moment in Five Families about the bat, an animal that flies but is not a bird.

check.q: A bat flies. Which family do they belong to?
options: Birds, because they fly
Mammals, because they have fur and feed their babies milk
Reptiles, because their wings have skin
check.why: Bats have fur and feed their babies milk, so they are mammals. They make their own heat too. Picking 'birds' means sorting by flying, but many things fly, even insects. Families are sorted by skin, breathing and babies.

flow.do: Count the points and name a winner. Then ask the question below.
flow.say: Well played. Now two last questions. Which family was hardest to fill, and why? Which animals surprised you?
flow.kid: Count your points. Who won? Which family was hardest? Which animal surprised you?
flow.context: This is the end of Five Families. Players count points and talk about the trickiest family.

good: The caecilian, because they look like a worm but are an amphibian.
The dolphin, because they live in water but breathe air.

games.title: Sun, Shade and Snow
games.players: 2 or more players, best outdoors or in a big room
games.context: This is a running game about keeping warm and cool. Some players are lizards, who take heat from outside. Some are sparrows, who make their own heat.

printables.title: 8 role cards (4 LIZARD, 4 SPARROW; use as many as you have players)

rules: Mark a SUN corner and a SHADE corner with a chunni or a chalk line.

One player is the caller and shows the weather cards. Everyone else takes a role card: LIZARD or SPARROW. With 2 players, the other player is a lizard for the first 10 cards, then you swap: the caller becomes a sparrow and the other player calls.
Each sparrow starts with 2 food tokens. The rest stay in a pile.
The caller shuffles the 6 weather cards and shows them one by one, calling each out loud. After the last, shuffle and go on until 10 cards have been shown. Players act out each one.
SUNNY MORNING: lizards run to the SUN corner to bask. Sparrows can play anywhere, and each one picks up a food token from the pile.
HOT NOON: lizards run to SHADE. Sparrows pant with open mouths.
COLD NIGHT, WINTER WIND or SNOW: lizards freeze still until the next card. Sparrows puff up and huddle, and each sparrow gives one food token back to the pile to keep warm.
MONSOON RAIN: lizards and sparrows both run to SHADE to shelter from the rain.
A sparrow with no token to give on a cold card must sit out the next card. A lizard that moves on a cold card sits out the next card.
After 10 weather cards, stop. There is no winner. Talk about who did better in each kind of weather.

setup.art: A courtyard with a sunny corner marked by a yellow chunni and a shady corner under a tree, children holding LIZARD and SPARROW cards.
setup.caption: 1. Mark a sun corner and a shade corner. Give out role cards.

setup.art: A parent holding up a card with a snowflake while child lizards freeze still and child sparrows huddle together.
setup.caption: 2. The caller shows weather. Everyone acts it out.

flow.do: 1. Mark the SUN corner and the SHADE corner. 2. Give each player a role card. 3. Give each sparrow 2 food tokens.
flow.say: Lizards take their heat from outside, from the sun. Sparrows make their own heat inside, from food. Let's see how each one copes with the weather.
flow.kid: Are you a lizard or a sparrow? Lizards need the sun. Sparrows need food to stay warm.
flow.context: This is the first step of Sun, Shade and Snow, a running game about keeping warm. Here you set up the corners and the roles.

flow.do: Show the weather cards one by one. Call out each one loudly. After every SUNNY MORNING, give each sparrow one food token. After every COLD NIGHT, WINTER WIND or SNOW card, collect one food token from each sparrow. Stop after 10 cards.
flow.say: Sunny morning! Hot noon! Cold night! Remember, sparrows, you must spend a grain to stay warm in the cold.
flow.kid: Listen for the weather. Act it out fast. Sparrows, give a grain in the cold.
flow.context: This is the main part of Sun, Shade and Snow. The caller shows weather cards and players act out how their animal copes.

check.q: Game moment: COLD NIGHT. What does a lizard do?
options: Runs around to warm up
Stays still and slow until the sun comes
Eats lots of food to make heat
check.why: A lizard takes their heat from outside. On a cold night they simply go slow and still, and wait. Picking 'eats food to make heat' is what a sparrow does. Picking 'runs around' is what we do when we feel cold.

flow.do: Stop the game and ask the questions below.
flow.say: Who had a harder time in the snow, lizards or sparrows? Who needed more food?
flow.kid: Who did better in the cold? Who needed food? Say what you think.
flow.context: This is the last step of Sun, Shade and Snow. Players talk about which animal did better in which weather.

ask.q: Why did sparrows need food tokens but lizards did not?
good: Sparrows make their own heat, and that burns food.
Lizards just wait for the sun, so they save food.

ask.q: Who could still move on a cold night?
good: The sparrows, because they make their own heat.

flow.parent: The point of the game is the trade. Making your own heat lets you stay active in the cold, but it costs lots of food. Taking heat from outside saves food, but you must wait for the sun.

experiments.title: The Fur Coat Test: does a coat keep warmth in?
experiments.question: Does a woollen coat help a warm bottle stay warm for longer, the way fur and feathers help a warm animal?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. After 20 minutes, which bottle will be warmest: the bare one, the one in a dry woollen sock, or the one in a wet woollen sock? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, keep everything the same except the coat. Use the same bottles, the same amount of the same warm water, and the same place. Measure all three at the same times.

materials.item: 3 small plastic bottles of the same size, about 200 to 300 millilitres, with lids (not double-walled flasks)
warm tap water, not boiling, poured by a grown-up
2 woollen socks of the same thickness
a thermometer that can go in water (a digital fever thermometer works too, see the note in step 2)
a measuring cup
a clock or timer, and the results table

experiments.safety: A grown-up pours the warm water. It should feel comfortably warm to touch, like a bath, never hot enough to burn.

schedule.what: Fill three bottles with warm water. Dress one in a dry sock and one in a wet sock. Measure all three every 5 minutes for 20 minutes. Then draw a chart.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then work out how much each bottle cooled, by taking the last reading away from the first. Draw a bar for each bottle.
experiments.context: This is the fur coat test. Three bottles of warm water stand in for three warm animals. One has no coat, one has a dry woollen coat, and one has a wet coat. A thermometer shows which one stays warm longest.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: how many degrees each bottle cooled in 20 minutes
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different. A shorter bar means the bottle kept its warmth better.

setup.art: Three identical small plastic bottles on a table: one bare, one in a dry woollen sock, one in a wet woollen sock, a thermometer beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Fill three bottles with the same warm water. Give one a dry sock and one a wet sock.

setup.art: A child lifting a bottle lid and dipping a thermometer into the water while looking at a clock on the wall.
setup.caption: 2. Every 5 minutes, measure each bottle with the thermometer.

setup.art: A child writing numbers into a table with three rows, the three bottles drawn beside it.
setup.caption: 3. Write down every reading. Which bottle cooled least?

flow.do: Show your child a woollen sweater. Ask the questions below.
flow.say: On a cold morning, we put on a sweater. Does the sweater make heat, like a heater? Or does it do something else?
flow.kid: Hold a woollen sweater. Does it make heat? Or does it do something else?
flow.context: This is the start of the fur coat test. It begins by asking what a sweater, fur or feathers really do.

check.q: A woollen sweater keeps you warm. What does it really do?
options: It makes its own heat, like a small heater
It holds in the heat your body makes
It soaks up heat from the sun
check.why: Wool makes no heat. It traps still air, which holds in the heat your body makes. Picking 'makes heat' is very common, because a sweater feels warm when you put it on. But a sweater left on a chair stays as cold as the room.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up fills the three bottles with the same amount of warm water, using the measuring cup. 2. Put the lids on. 3. Put one bottle into a dry sock. 4. Soak the other sock in tap water, squeeze it until it stops dripping, and put the third bottle in it.
flow.say: These bottles are our pretend animals. The warm water is their body heat. One has no fur. One has a dry fur coat. One has a wet coat, like a dog that has jumped in a pond.
flow.kid: Three bottles are three animals. One has no coat. One has a dry coat. One has a wet coat.
flow.context: This is step 2 of the fur coat test. Here you fill the bottles and dress two of them in socks.
flow.parent: Use water at about 45 °C: hot-bath warm, so you can keep a finger in it. Measure each bottle at the start. They should all be within one degree. No water thermometer? A digital fever thermometer works if the water starts at about 42 °C, because most read only between 32 and 42 °C. Dip only the tip, and wash it well afterwards. Do not use a steel flask with two walls: it keeps heat in so well that you will see almost no change.

flow.do: Put the thermometer in each bottle in turn and write the starting temperature in the table.
flow.say: Let's read the thermometer. The number tells us how warm the water is, in degrees Celsius.
flow.kid: Put the thermometer in each bottle. Read the number. Write it down.
flow.context: This is step 3 of the fur coat test. Here you measure how warm each bottle is at the start.
flow.parent: Wait until the number stops changing before you read it. Put the lid back on quickly after each reading.

flow.do: Every 5 minutes (at 5, 10, 15 and 20 minutes), measure all three bottles and write the numbers in the table. Between readings, look at the questions below.
flow.say: Every five minutes we measure again. While we wait, think. Which animals have the thickest coats? Which animals must not get their fur wet?
flow.kid: Measure every 5 minutes, 4 times. While you wait, think. Which animals have thick coats?
flow.context: This is the waiting part of the fur coat test. You measure all three bottles every 5 minutes for 20 minutes.

good: Yaks in Ladakh
Sheep
Snow leopards
Puffed-up pigeons in winter

ask.q: Why do ducks oil their feathers?
good: So the water rolls off and their feathers stay dry and warm.

flow.parent: The bottles differ by only a few degrees, so wait for the number to settle before you read it.

flow.do: Work out how much each bottle cooled. Take the last reading away from the first. Draw a bar for each bottle.
flow.say: Let's see which bottle lost the least heat. Take the last number away from the first number, for each bottle.
flow.kid: For each bottle, take the last number from the first. That is how much it cooled.
flow.context: This is step 5 of the fur coat test. Here you work out how much each bottle cooled in 20 minutes.

check.q: Which bottle usually cools the least?
options: The bare bottle
The bottle in the dry woollen sock
The bottle in the wet woollen sock
check.why: The dry wool traps still air, and still air lets heat out slowly. So that bottle stays warmest. Picking the wet sock usually means thinking 'more covering is always better'. But in wet wool, water fills the gaps where the air was, and the drying water carries heat away. That is why a wet animal gets cold so fast.

flow.parent: The dry sock bottle may be only 1 or 2 degrees warmer than the bare one, and the wet sock result can change with the room. That is fine: write down what you really measured.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me what you found out, in three parts. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.context: This is the last step of the fur coat test. You say what you found out, like a scientist.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this (with the made-up numbers from the chart). What I think: a dry coat holds warmth in. What I saw: the bare bottle cooled 6 degrees, the dry sock bottle cooled only 4, and the wet sock bottle cooled 9. Why: dry wool traps still air, like fur and feathers. Wet wool does not, and the drying water takes heat away. Notice too that even the dry sock bottle kept cooling. A coat slows heat leaving, but never stops it.

experiments.title: Lizard on a Wall: sun or shade?
experiments.question: How much does the sun warm something that cannot make its own heat?
experiments.predict: Guess. After 30 minutes, how much warmer will the tumbler in the sun be than the one in the shade? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use two tumblers that are the same. Fill them with the same amount of water from the same tap at the same time. Change only one thing: one goes in the sun, one in the shade.

materials.item: 2 identical steel tumblers
cool tap water
a thermometer that can go in water (a fever thermometer will not work here, because cool water is below its lowest reading)
a spot in direct sunlight, such as a balcony ledge or an open window, and a shady spot close to it
the results table

experiments.safety: Do not look at the sun. If you use a balcony ledge, a grown-up stays with you.

schedule.what: Fill two tumblers with cool water. Put one in the sun and one in the shade. Measure both every 15 minutes for half an hour. Then compare.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Work out how much each tumbler warmed. Draw two bars.
experiments.context: This is the lizard on a wall test. Two steel tumblers of cool water stand in for two lizards. One lies in the sun and one hides in the shade. A thermometer shows how much the sun warms them.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: how much each tumbler warmed in 30 minutes
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up. Your numbers will depend on the weather.

setup.art: Two identical steel tumblers of water, one on a bright sunny windowsill and one on a shady shelf, a thermometer between them.
setup.caption: 1. Fill two tumblers with cool water. Put one in the sun and one in the shade.

setup.art: A child dipping a thermometer into the sunny tumbler, a clock behind showing 15 minutes passed.
setup.caption: 2. Measure both every 15 minutes.

setup.art: A lizard basking on a sunny wall beside the warm tumbler.
setup.caption: 3. Compare. This is how a lizard warms up.

flow.do: Ask your child about the house lizard at home, or show a picture of a lizard basking on a wall. Ask the question below.
flow.say: A lizard cannot make much heat of their own. Their body is about as warm as the air or the wall they sit on. In the morning, many lizards lie in the sun. How much do you think the sun can warm something like that?
flow.kid: A lizard is as warm as the things around them. How much can the sun warm them? Let's test it.
flow.context: This is the start of the lizard on a wall test. It begins by thinking about how lizards warm up.

ask.q: Why does a lizard lie in the sun?
good: To get warm.
They cannot make much heat of their own, so they take the sun's.

flow.do: 1. Fill both tumblers with the same amount of cool tap water. 2. Measure both and write the start temperature. 3. Put one in the sun and one in the shade.
flow.say: Each tumbler is a pretend lizard. Like a lizard, a tumbler cannot make heat. It can only take heat from around it.
flow.kid: Fill both tumblers. Measure them. Put one in the sun. Put one in the shade.
flow.context: This is step 2 of the lizard on a wall test. Here you set up the two tumblers.

flow.do: Measure both tumblers after 15 minutes and after 30 minutes. In between, do something else, like reading the story or playing a game.
flow.say: Now we wait. A lizard waits too. They cannot hurry the sun.
flow.kid: Now wait. Check at 15 minutes and 30 minutes. Write the numbers.
flow.context: This is the waiting part of the lizard on a wall test. You measure both tumblers twice.

check.q: After 30 minutes, which tumbler is likely to be warmer?
options: The one in the shade, because it is cooler there
The one in the sun
They will be the same, because the water is the same
check.why: The sunny tumbler takes in the sun's warmth, just as a basking lizard does. Picking 'the same' means forgetting that a thing that cannot make its own heat warms up and cools down with its surroundings.

flow.parent: Put the sunny tumbler where the sun falls straight on it, not through window glass, which blocks some of the warmth. No thermometer? Dip one finger in each tumbler at the end. The sunny one should feel warmer. On a cloudy day, the difference will be small. Try again on a sunny day.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me what you found out, in three parts. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.context: This is the last step of the lizard on a wall test. You say what you found out, like a scientist.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: things that cannot make their own heat get warm from the sun. What I saw: the sunny tumbler went from 26 to 32 degrees, but the shady one only went to 28. Why: sunlight warms what it lands on. A lizard is warmed the same way.

experiments.title: Egg in the Air: why frogs lay eggs in water
experiments.question: Does a shell stop an egg from drying out in the air?
experiments.predict: Guess. After one day, which jelly egg clump will be the most dried up: the one in the open, the one in water, or the one inside an eggshell? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same amount of soaked sabja seeds in each place. Keep all three in the same room. Change only one thing: open air, water, or inside a shell.
results_table: How they look at the start
Still wet and soft? (yes or no)

materials.item: 2 teaspoons of sabja seeds (basil seeds), soaked in water for 15 minutes
3 small steel bowls
two halves of a cracked eggshell, washed, from the kitchen (no eggs at home? use a small steel box with its lid on)
a little sticky tape
a magnifying glass, if you have one

experiments.safety: Wash your hands after touching raw eggshell. Do not eat the seeds after the test.

schedule.what: Soak the sabja seeds. Put one spoonful in an open bowl, one in a bowl of water, and one inside an eggshell taped shut. Look again after 3 hours.
Look at all three again. Which jelly eggs are still soft and wet? Then say what you found out.

experiments.record: Draw how each clump looks at the start, after 3 hours and after 1 day.
experiments.context: This is the egg in the air test. Soaked sabja seeds look and feel like frog eggs: tiny black dots in clear jelly. We see what happens to jelly eggs in open air, in water, and inside an eggshell.

setup.art: Soaked sabja seeds in a spoon, each tiny black seed inside a clear ball of jelly, like frogspawn.
setup.caption: 1. Soak sabja seeds. They look like frog eggs in jelly.

setup.art: Three steel bowls: one with jelly seeds in the open, one with seeds under water, one with an eggshell taped shut.
setup.caption: 2. Put one spoonful in the open, one in water, one inside a shell.

setup.art: A child looking through a magnifying glass at a dried, crusty clump of seeds next to a still-wet clump.
setup.caption: 3. After a day, which jelly eggs dried out?

flow.do: Soak 2 teaspoons of sabja seeds in a cup of water for 15 minutes, then pour off the extra water. Look at the seeds with the magnifying glass.
flow.say: Look. Each little black seed now sits in a ball of clear jelly. Frog eggs look just like this: a dark dot in a ball of jelly.
flow.kid: Soak the seeds. Look with the lens. Each seed sits in a ball of jelly, like a frog egg.
flow.context: This is the start of the egg in the air test. You soak sabja seeds so they look like frog eggs.

flow.do: 1. Put one spoonful of jelly seeds in an open bowl. 2. Put one spoonful in a bowl of water. 3. Put one spoonful inside half an eggshell, cover it with the other half and tape it shut. Put it in the third bowl.
flow.say: Frogs lay their eggs in water. Hens lay their eggs in a dry nest, with a shell. Let's see why.
flow.kid: Put one spoonful in the open bowl. Put one in water. Put one inside an eggshell, and tape it shut.
flow.context: This is step 2 of the egg in the air test. Here you put the jelly eggs in three different places.
flow.parent: A steel box keeps in even more water than a real shell, because a real shell has tiny holes that let air through. In very humid weather, the open spoonful dries slowly. Put all three bowls under a fan.

flow.do: After 3 hours, and again the next day, look at all three. Open the eggshell carefully.
flow.say: Which jelly eggs are still soft and wet? Which are drying out?
flow.kid: Look at all three. Which are still wet? Which dried up?
flow.context: This is step 3 of the egg in the air test. You check the jelly eggs after 3 hours and after a day.

check.q: Which jelly eggs dried out the most?
options: The ones in water
The ones in the open bowl
The ones inside the eggshell
check.why: Out in the open air, water leaves the jelly and it dries into a crust. In water, it stays soft. Inside the shell, much less water escapes. Picking the shell usually means thinking a shell is just for protection. It also keeps the egg from drying out, so birds and reptiles can lay eggs on dry land.

flow.wait: Leave it until the next day

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me what you found out, in three parts. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.context: This is the last step of the egg in the air test. You say what you found out, like a scientist.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: jelly eggs need water, but a shell keeps an egg moist in air. What I saw: the open seeds dried into a crust, but the ones in water and in the shell stayed soft. Why: water escapes from jelly into dry air. The shell slows that down. That is why frogs lay eggs in water and hens can lay eggs in a dry nest.

activities.title: The Spoon in Your Fist

materials.item: 2 steel spoons from the kitchen drawer, at room temperature

schedule.what: Hold a steel spoon in your fist for 3 minutes. Feel it warm up. Ask where the warmth came from.

activities.record: Draw your fist and the spoon. Draw arrows to show which way the warmth moved.
activities.context: This is a short noticing activity. You hold a steel spoon in your fist and feel it warm up. It shows that your body makes heat, and a spoon does not.

setup.art: A child's hand closing around the bowl of a steel spoon, a second steel spoon lying on the table beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Take two steel spoons. Hold one tight in your fist.

setup.art: After three minutes, the child opening the fist and touching the spoon to a cheek, the other spoon still on the table.
setup.caption: 2. After 3 minutes, open your hand. Compare the two spoons.

flow.do: Give your child two steel spoons that have been lying in the room. Ask them to touch both to their cheek.
flow.say: Touch both spoons to your cheek. How do they feel? Now hold one spoon tight in your fist. Keep the other on the table.
flow.kid: Touch both spoons to your cheek. Cool? Now hold one tight in your fist.
flow.context: This is the start of the spoon in your fist. You feel two steel spoons, then hold one in your hand.

flow.do: Wait 3 minutes. Then ask your child to open the fist and touch both spoons to their cheek again.
flow.say: Now open your hand. Touch both spoons to your cheek again. What do you notice? What do you wonder?
flow.kid: Open your hand. Touch both spoons to your cheek. What do you notice?
flow.context: This is the noticing step of the spoon in your fist. After 3 minutes, you compare the held spoon with the other one.

good: The spoon from my hand is warm.
The other spoon is still cool.
Where did the warmth come from?
Can a spoon make heat?

check.q: The spoon in your fist got warm. Where did the warmth come from?
options: The spoon made it
Your hand made it, and it moved into the spoon
The air in the room made it
check.why: Your body makes heat from the food you eat. Some of that heat moved from your hand into the spoon. Picking 'the spoon made it' is a common first guess. But the spoon on the table stayed cool. A spoon cannot make its own heat.

flow.do: Ask the question below. Then tell your child what the unit will explore.
flow.say: Some animals are like your hand. They make their own heat. Others are more like the spoon. They warm up only when something warm is near them, like the sun. Which animals do you think are like the spoon?
flow.kid: Some animals make heat, like your hand. Some are like the spoon. They need the sun. Guess which ones.
flow.context: This is the last step of the spoon in your fist. It links the spoon to animals that make their own heat and animals that do not.

ask.q: Which animals might be like the spoon?
good: Lizards, like the house lizard on our wall.
Snakes.
Frogs and fish.

flow.think: Is a lizard on a cold morning more like your hand or more like the spoon?

activities.title: Backbone Spotting from Home

materials.item: a notebook and pencil
a spotting chart with five columns (fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, mammals), drawn in the notebook in step 1

activities.safety: Watch animals from a window, a balcony or the building's gate. Never touch street dogs, stray cats or birds. At the market, stay with a grown-up.

schedule.what: Spend 20 minutes at a window or balcony. Tick each animal with a backbone you see, and write how they were keeping warm or cool. Extra, next time you are at a fish stall: look at the fish's gills and tick the fish too.

activities.record: Tick every vertebrate you see in their group. Next to each, write one thing they were doing to keep warm or cool.
activities.context: This is a spotting activity for animals with backbones that live around a city home: crows, pigeons, house lizards, dogs, cats, the fish at the market, and people. You sort them into the five groups and watch how each one keeps warm or cool.

setup.art: A parent and child at a flat's window with a notebook, pointing at a crow on a wire and pigeons on the ledge, a house lizard on the wall inside.
setup.caption: 1. Watch from a window or balcony. Look for animals with backbones.

setup.art: A notebook page with five columns marked by small drawings of a fish, a frog, a lizard, a bird and a dog, with ticks in each.
setup.caption: 2. Tick each animal in their group.

setup.art: A fish on ice at a market stall, their gill cover lifted to show red gills, with a child looking closely.
setup.caption: 3. Extra: at a fish stall, look at a fish's gills.

flow.do: Draw the five columns in the notebook. Sit at a window or on the balcony together.
flow.say: Today we are animal spotters. We only count animals with a backbone. For each one, we look at what they are doing to stay warm or cool.
flow.kid: You are an animal spotter. Count animals with a backbone. Watch how they keep warm or cool.
flow.context: This is the start of backbone spotting. You get your chart ready at a window or balcony.

flow.do: Watch for about 20 minutes. Tick each vertebrate in the right column and note what they are doing.
flow.say: Look, a crow. Which group? Are they in the sun or the shade? Is there a house lizard on our wall? Where are they sitting?
flow.kid: Spot an animal. Which group? Tick them. Are they in sun or shade?
flow.context: This is the main part of backbone spotting. You spot animals, sort them and watch how they keep warm or cool.

good: Basking on a sunny wall.
Hidden behind a frame or a cupboard on a cold day.

ask.q: What are the dogs or cats doing in the heat?
good: Lying in the shade.
Panting.

flow.parent: Crows, pigeons, mynas and sparrows are birds. Dogs, cats, squirrels, bats at dusk and people are mammals. The house lizard is a reptile. Extra: at a fish stall, lift a fish's gill cover to see the red gills, and tick the fish. Frogs are hard to find in a city, except near puddles in the monsoon. An empty amphibian column is a real finding: frogs need damp places, and a city has few.

flow.do: Count the ticks in each column and talk about the questions below.
flow.say: Which group did we see most? Which group was hardest to find? Why do you think that is?
flow.kid: Count your ticks. Which group did you see most? Which was hardest to find?
flow.context: This is the last step of backbone spotting. You count what you found and think about why.

check.q: In the monsoon you saw a frog sitting in a wet drain on a hot day. Why might they stay there?
options: Frogs like dirty water
Frogs must keep their skin damp, because they breathe through it
Frogs cannot see the dry ground
check.why: A frog breathes partly through their thin skin, and the skin only works when it is damp. A wet drain also keeps them cool. Picking 'dirty water' misses the real reason. The frog is looking for wet, not dirt.

activities.title: Cool Down Like Them

materials.item: a bowl of tap water
a hand fan or a folded newspaper
a big leaf or a sheet of paper cut into an elephant-ear shape

activities.safety: Keep the water away from electric sockets.

schedule.what: Try three animal ways to keep cool: sweating, panting and flapping ears.

activities.record: Write which wrist felt cooler, and why. Draw one animal and their way of keeping cool.
activities.context: This activity tries three ways animals keep cool: sweating like people and horses, panting like dogs, and flapping big ears like elephants.

setup.art: A child with one wet wrist and one dry wrist held up in front of a hand fan.
setup.caption: 1. Wet one wrist. Fan both wrists.

setup.art: A child panting with tongue out beside a cartoon dog doing the same.
setup.caption: 2. Pant like a dog for ten seconds.

setup.art: A child flapping a big paper elephant ear made from newspaper.
setup.caption: 3. Flap a paper elephant ear.

flow.do: 1. Dip one wrist in water. Keep the other dry. 2. Fan both wrists for 30 seconds. 3. Ask which feels cooler.
flow.say: Let's be people and horses first. We sweat. Wet one wrist and fan both. Which one feels cooler?
flow.kid: Wet one wrist. Fan both. Which one feels cooler?
flow.context: This is the first part of cool down like them. You test how wet skin cools, the way sweat does.

check.q: Which wrist feels cooler when you fan them?
options: The dry wrist
The wet wrist
Both feel the same
check.why: When water dries off your skin, it carries heat away with it. That is how sweating cools you. Picking 'both the same' usually means thinking the fan does all the cooling. The fan only helps the water dry faster.

flow.do: Ask your child to pant quickly with an open mouth for ten seconds, then notice how their tongue and mouth feel.
flow.say: Dogs hardly sweat. So they pant. Fast breaths dry the water off their tongue and mouth, and that carries heat away.
flow.kid: Dogs can't sweat much. They pant. Pant for ten seconds. Does your tongue feel cooler and drier?
flow.context: This is the second part of cool down like them. You pant like a dog.

flow.do: Make a big elephant ear from a sheet of newspaper. Flap it next to your face for 30 seconds.
flow.say: Elephants have huge, thin ears full of blood vessels. When they flap them, the moving air cools the blood. Then the cool blood flows back into the body. Buffaloes cannot sweat much either, so what do they do?
flow.kid: Flap a paper elephant ear. Feel the breeze? Elephants cool their blood this way.
flow.context: This is the third part of cool down like them. You flap a big paper ear like an elephant.

ask.q: What does a buffalo do on a hot day?
good: They lie in mud or water.
The wet mud dries and cools them.
They go into the shade or a crack in the wall.

activities.title: Big Body, Small Body

materials.item: one big bottle, about 1 litre
one small bottle, about 200 millilitres
warm tap water, poured by a grown-up
a thermometer

activities.safety: A grown-up pours the warm water. It should feel warm, like a bath, not hot.

schedule.what: Fill a big and a small bottle with the same warm water. Measure both at the start, then every 10 minutes for half an hour.

activities.record: Write the temperatures in a table. Work out how much each bottle cooled.
activities.context: This activity compares a big and a small bottle of warm water. It shows why small animals, like mice and sunbirds, lose heat faster than big ones, like elephants.

setup.art: A big bottle and a small bottle filled with warm water on a table, a thermometer between them, an elephant drawn next to the big one and a mouse next to the small one.
setup.caption: 1. Fill a big and a small bottle with the same warm water.

setup.art: A child reading the thermometer in the small bottle with a clock behind showing 10 minutes passed.
setup.caption: 2. Measure both every 10 minutes. Which cools faster?

flow.do: A grown-up fills both bottles with the same warm water. Measure the start temperature of each.
flow.say: The big bottle is an elephant. The small bottle is a mouse. Both start just as warm. Which do you think will cool down faster?
flow.kid: Big bottle is an elephant. Small bottle is a mouse. Which will cool faster? Guess.
flow.context: This is the start of big body, small body. You fill a big and a small bottle with warm water.

flow.do: Measure both after 10, 20 and 30 minutes. Write the numbers down.
flow.say: Every ten minutes, we check. In between we can play Five Families or read the story.
flow.kid: Measure both bottles every 10 minutes. Write the numbers down.
flow.context: This is the waiting part of big body, small body. You measure both bottles three times.

flow.do: Work out how much each cooled. Ask the questions below.
flow.say: Which one cooled faster? So which animal needs to make heat faster, to stay warm: the mouse or the elephant?
flow.kid: Which bottle cooled faster? Which animal must eat more for their size?
flow.context: This is the last step of big body, small body. You compare how much each bottle cooled.

check.q: The small bottle usually cools faster. What does this tell us about small animals?
options: Small animals stay warm more easily
Small animals lose heat fast, so they must eat a lot for their size
Size makes no difference
check.why: A small body has lots of skin for its size, so heat escapes quickly. That is why a tiny sunbird or a mouse eats almost all day. Picking 'stay warm more easily' mixes up 'small' with 'cosy'. An elephant has the opposite problem. It must work to cool down.

activities.title: My Steady Warmth: a three-day body temperature diary

materials.item: the family's digital fever thermometer, for your body
a thermometer for the air (or the outdoor temperature on a phone weather app)
a diary table drawn in the notebook: day, time, air (°C), my body (°C)

schedule.what: Measure your body temperature and the air temperature in the morning and the evening.
Measure again. Then compare: did your body change as much as the air?

activities.record: Fill in a table with four columns: day, time, air (°C), my body (°C).
activities.context: This is a three-day diary. Each morning and evening you measure the air and your own body. It shows how a body that makes its own heat stays steady while the air changes.

setup.art: A child holding a digital fever thermometer under the arm, with a second thermometer on the windowsill measuring the air.
setup.caption: 1. Measure the air. Then measure yourself.

setup.art: A simple diary table with a sun and a moon symbol for each day, and two columns of numbers.
setup.caption: 2. Write both numbers, morning and evening, for three days.

flow.do: Measure the air: leave the water thermometer on a windowsill for 3 minutes, or read the outdoor temperature on a phone. Then measure your child's temperature under the arm with the fever thermometer. Write both down.
flow.say: First we measure the air. Then we measure you. Let's do this every morning and every evening for three days.
flow.kid: Measure the air. Then measure you. Write both numbers.
flow.context: This is the daily step of my steady warmth. You measure the air and your body, morning and evening.
flow.parent: A healthy child's temperature under the arm is usually around 36 to 37 °C. If it is 37.5 °C or more under the arm, the child may have a fever. Clean the thermometer before and after each use, and measure only under the arm.

flow.do: Repeat on day 2 and day 3, at the same times.
flow.say: Same times as yesterday. Morning and evening.
flow.kid: Measure again, at the same times as yesterday.
flow.context: This is the second and third day of my steady warmth. You measure again at the same times.
flow.wait: Do this again on the next two days

flow.do: On day 3, look at all the numbers together. Ask the questions below.
flow.say: How much did the air change from morning to evening? How much did your body change?
flow.kid: Look at your numbers. Did the air change a lot? Did you?
flow.context: This is the last step of my steady warmth. You compare how much the air and your body changed.

check.q: The air changed by 8 degrees. Your body changed by less than 1 degree. Why?
options: The thermometer is broken
Your body makes its own heat and keeps itself steady
You stayed indoors all day
check.why: Mammals and birds keep their bodies at almost the same warmth, day and night. Your body makes more heat when it is cold and sweats when it is hot. Picking 'stayed indoors' is a fair thought, but even outdoors your body stays near 37 °C. A lizard's body would have changed with the air.

activities.title: Who Looks After the Babies?

materials.item: a large sheet of paper
crayons or colour pencils
the animal cards from Five Families

schedule.what: Make a chart of five animals: how many eggs or babies they have, and how much the parents care for them.

activities.record: A chart with one row for each animal: the animal, eggs or babies, about how many, and who looks after them.
activities.context: In this activity you make a chart comparing how five animals have young: a fish, a frog, a turtle, a bird and a mammal. You find a pattern between the number of babies and the care they get.

setup.art: A big sheet of paper divided into five rows, each with a small drawing of a rohu, a frog, a turtle, a sparrow and a cow.
setup.caption: 1. Draw five rows, one for each group.

setup.art: A child drawing many tiny eggs in the fish row and one calf with their mother in the cow row.
setup.caption: 2. Draw how many eggs or babies, and who cares for them.

flow.do: Draw five rows: rohu fish, frog, olive ridley turtle, house sparrow, cow. Read out the facts below and fill in the chart together.
flow.say: A rohu lays lakhs of eggs and swims away. A frog lays hundreds or thousands of jelly eggs and leaves them. An olive ridley turtle lays about a hundred eggs in the sand and goes back to the sea. A sparrow lays three to five eggs and feeds her chicks. A cow has one calf and feeds them milk for months.
flow.kid: Fill in the chart. How many eggs or babies? Who looks after them?
flow.context: This is the start of who looks after the babies. You fill in a chart of five animals.

flow.do: Look at the chart together and ask the questions below.
flow.say: Look at the numbers. Which animals have the most babies? Which ones look after their babies most? Do you see a pattern?
flow.kid: Look at the chart. Many babies, or few? Lots of care, or none? See a pattern?
flow.context: This is the pattern step of who looks after the babies. You look for a link between how many babies and how much care.

options: Animals with many eggs care for each one a lot
Animals with many eggs usually leave them, and animals with few young care for them
All animals care for their babies the same amount
check.why: Making and caring for a baby costs a parent food and time. So there is a trade. Lots of eggs and little care, or few babies and lots of care. Picking 'the same amount' misses the pattern. Picking the first one mixes the two sides up.

flow.do: Tell your child about the mugger crocodile, the king cobra and the emperor penguin. Add them to the chart.
flow.say: There are surprises in every group. A mugger crocodile guards her nest and carries her babies to the water in her mouth. A king cobra builds a nest of leaves. A father emperor penguin holds his egg on his feet for two months.
flow.kid: Some reptiles care for babies too. Mugger crocodiles carry babies in their mouths. Add them to the chart.
flow.context: This is the last step of who looks after the babies. You add some surprising animal parents to the chart.

projects.title: Nest Builder: keep the egg warm

materials.item: a small bottle, about 200 millilitres, as the egg
warm tap water, poured by a grown-up
nest materials from home: cotton wool, old cloth, wool scraps, newspaper, a few dry leaves from a potted plant
a thermometer
a cardboard box or a steel bowl as the base

projects.safety: A grown-up pours the warm water. Do not pick up feathers or old nests, because they can carry mites.

schedule.what: Collect nest materials at home. Look for a pigeon nest on a balcony, window ledge or air-conditioner box, from a distance.
Build your nest around a warm water egg. Measure how warm it stays after 20 minutes. Compare with a bare egg.

projects.record: Draw your nest and label what you used. Write the egg's temperature at the start and after 20 minutes, with and without your nest.
projects.context: In this two-day project you build a nest that keeps a warm water egg warm, the way birds keep their eggs warm. Then you test it with a thermometer.

setup.art: A child gathering cotton wool, a strip of old cloth and wool scraps into a box at home, a pigeon nest of twigs visible on a ledge outside.
setup.caption: 1. Collect cotton wool, cloth, wool and paper.

setup.art: A small warm-water bottle nestled in a round nest of grass and cotton wool inside a bowl.
setup.caption: 2. Build a nest around a warm water egg.

setup.art: Two bottles side by side, one bare and one in the nest, with a thermometer and a clock.
setup.caption: 3. After 20 minutes, which egg is warmer?

flow.do: Collect dry, soft nest materials at home. Then look out of the windows and balconies for a pigeon nest. Do not touch it.
flow.say: Birds must keep their eggs warm, or the babies inside will not grow. So they build nests and sit on them. Let's collect things a bird might use, and look for a real nest.
flow.kid: Collect soft, dry things. Look for a pigeon nest. Don't touch it.
flow.context: This is day 1 of nest builder. You collect materials and look for a real nest.
flow.parent: Pigeons often nest on balconies, window ledges and air-conditioner boxes. Their nests are a loose pile of twigs. If you have a park nearby, you may also see sparrow nests in wall gaps or weaver bird nests hanging from trees.

flow.do: A grown-up fills two small bottles with the same warm water. Build a nest around one bottle. Leave the other bare. Measure both at the start and after 20 minutes.
flow.say: Now build a nest around your egg. Think. What kept the bottle warm in the fur coat test?
flow.kid: Build a nest round one warm bottle. Leave one bare. Measure both after 20 minutes.
flow.context: This is day 2 of nest builder. You build a nest and test whether it keeps the egg warm.

check.q: Which nest material is likely to work best?
options: A few hard twigs with big gaps
Soft, fluffy things that trap air, like cotton wool or feathers
Wet grass
check.why: Fluffy things trap still air, and still air slows heat from escaping. Picking twigs with big gaps lets the wind blow through. Picking wet grass forgets the fur coat test, where the wet sock cooled fastest.

flow.do: Compare the two eggs. Improve your nest and test again if you have time.
flow.say: How many degrees warmer is your nested egg? How could you make the nest better? A real bird adds one more thing. What is it?
flow.kid: Which egg stayed warmer? How can you make your nest better?
flow.context: This is the last step of nest builder. You compare and improve your nest.

ask.q: What does a real bird add that our nest does not have?
good: Their own warm body sitting on the eggs.
Their feathers on top.

challenges.title: Save the Ice Cube
challenges.problem: Fur keeps heat in. Can it keep heat out too? Your job is to stop an ice cube from melting for as long as you can, using things from home.
constraints: You may not put it in the fridge.
You may only use things you find at home.
Each cube must sit in the same room, on the same table.
materials: small steel bowls or plastic cups
things from home, like a woollen sock, cotton wool, newspaper, aluminium foil, a cloth, a thermos flask lid
general: Wrap the cube in a woollen sock or cotton wool, so still air slows the room's heat getting in.
Wrap it in shiny foil, which bounces back some heat.
Keep it in the shade, away from the sun and the stove.
creative: Camels have thick fur on their backs. It stops the desert sun from heating them. Could a thick 'camel coat' on top work best?
Put the cube in a cup, inside a bigger cup, with cotton wool between, like the double walls of a flask.
Try a layer of cotton wool and a layer of foil together.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own ice coat. Draw it, build it and time it. Did it beat the bare ice cube?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You build a coat that keeps an ice cube from melting, to find out if fur and feathers can keep heat out as well as in.

setup.art: A row of steel bowls with ice cubes, one bare, one in a woollen sock, one wrapped in foil and one in cotton wool.
setup.caption: 1. Put one bare ice cube out. Wrap the others in different coats.

setup.art: A child peeking into a woollen sock to check a still-solid ice cube next to a bowl with only a puddle.
setup.caption: 2. Check every 10 minutes. Which one lasts longest?

flow.do: Ask the question below. Then let your child choose materials.
flow.say: We found that wool keeps a warm bottle warm. Do you think it could keep an ice cube cold? Some people think a sweater would make it melt faster.
flow.kid: Will a woollen coat make ice melt faster, or slower? Guess first.
flow.context: This is the start of save the ice cube. You guess whether a coat keeps cold things cold.

check.q: What will a woollen sock do to an ice cube?
options: Melt it faster, because wool is warm
Slow down the melting, because wool slows heat moving in
Nothing at all
check.why: Wool is not warm by itself. It slows heat moving from one side to the other, in either direction. So it keeps the room's heat away from the ice. Picking 'melt it faster' is the most common guess, because we feel warm in sweaters. But the warmth was ours all along.

flow.do: Build the coats. Put all the cubes out at the same time. Check every 10 minutes and note which is melting.
flow.say: Let's check. Which one is a puddle? Which one is still a cube?
flow.kid: Check every 10 minutes. Which ice cube is melting fastest?
flow.context: This is the testing part of save the ice cube. You check each cube every 10 minutes.

flow.do: Talk about the winner and the questions below.
flow.say: Which coat won? How is that like a camel's fur in the desert sun?
flow.kid: Which coat won? How is a camel's fur like your coat?
flow.context: This is the last step of save the ice cube. You talk about which coat worked best and why.

ask.q: Why does a camel have thick fur in the hot desert?
good: To keep the sun's heat out in the day.
To keep warm on cold desert nights.

challenges.title: A Damp Home for a Frog
challenges.problem: Frogs breathe through their skin, so their skin must stay damp. Design a shady hideout that keeps a wet sponge damp for as long as possible in a sunny spot.
constraints: Use one kitchen sponge as the frog. Soak both sponges, then squeeze each until it stops dripping, so they hold the same water.
The hideout must fit inside a shoebox.
Place it in the same sunny spot as a bare wet sponge.
materials: a few leaves and a little soil from a potted plant, a small clay pot, a cloth, a plastic sheet
general: Make shade with leaves or a clay pot, so the sun cannot dry the sponge.
Put damp soil under it, like a frog burrowing.
Cover it so the wind cannot blow across it.
creative: The Indian purple frog of the Western Ghats lives deep underground for most of the year. Could you bury your frog?
A clay pot stays cool when wet, like a matka. Could a wet clay pot help?
Some frogs hide in tree holes full of rainwater. Could a small cup of water nearby keep the air damp?
challenges.your_turn: Design your own frog hideout. Draw it, build it, and weigh or squeeze the sponge after two hours. Which stayed wettest?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about amphibians. Frogs breathe through damp skin, so they must not dry out. You build a hideout that keeps a wet sponge frog damp in the sun.

flow.do: Read the problem together and look at the materials.
flow.say: A frog breathes through their skin, so their skin must stay damp. If it dries out, the frog is in danger. That is why frogs hide in the day and come out in the rain.
flow.kid: A frog's skin must stay wet. Build them a damp, shady home.
flow.context: This is the start of a damp home for a frog. You learn why frogs need damp places.

check.q: Why do frogs come out mostly at night and in the rain?
options: Because they are scared of the sun
Because damp, cool air keeps their skin from drying out
Because they cannot see in daylight
check.why: Frogs breathe partly through thin, damp skin. Sun and dry air would dry it out, so hiding by day keeps them safe. Picking 'scared' names a feeling but not the reason behind it. Picking 'cannot see' is not true. Many frogs see well by day.

flow.do: Build the hideout. Put it and a bare wet sponge in the sun. Wait two hours, doing other things.
flow.say: Let's build it and wait. Real frogs wait out the hot day too.
flow.kid: Build your hideout. Put it in the sun with a bare sponge. Wait two hours.
flow.context: This is the building part of a damp home for a frog.

flow.do: Squeeze each sponge over its own cup. Compare the water.
flow.say: Which sponge gave more water? If it was the one in your hideout, your hideout kept your frog damp.
flow.kid: Squeeze both sponges. Which gave more water?
flow.context: This is the last step of a damp home for a frog. You squeeze the sponges to see which stayed wetter.

items.p: A snake, a fish, a sparrow, a frog and a cow look very different. What do all five have?
items.why: All five are vertebrates, animals with a backbone. Many people guess 'legs', but snakes and fish have none. Fur belongs only to mammals, and gills only to fish and tadpoles.
items.art: Five animal outlines with a glowing backbone in each.

items.p: Sort these animals into their groups.
items.why: Sort by skin, breathing and babies, not by where an animal lives or whether they fly. The bat flies but has fur and milk, so they are a mammal. The dolphin lives in water but breathes air and feeds milk, so they are a mammal. The penguin cannot fly but has feathers, so they are a bird.

items.p: Watch a fish in a tank. The flaps just behind their eyes open and close all the time. What are the flaps doing?
opts: Pumping water over the gills, which take oxygen out of the water
items.why: Fish breathe with gills. The fish gulps water in at the mouth, and the water flows over the red gills and out under the flaps. Blood in the gills picks up oxygen from the water. Many people think fish do not breathe at all, because they never take a breath of air.

items.p: A frog breathes through their lungs and their damp ____.
items.why: Frogs breathe partly through their thin, wet skin. That is why they must stay damp.

items.p: Which two groups make their own body heat?
items.why: Birds and mammals make their own heat from food. Picking fish or reptiles is common, because some of them are warm in the sun. But that warmth comes from outside.

items.p: A lizard is slow on a cold morning because they are lazy.
items.why: False. A lizard takes their heat from outside. When their body is cold, their muscles work slowly. Once the sun warms them, they are quick.

items.p: Fur and feathers keep animals warm by trapping air.
items.why: True. Still air lets heat out very slowly. Fur and feathers hold a layer of still air next to the skin.

items.p: Match each animal to how they keep cool.
items.why: Each animal has their own way. Drying water carries heat away in sweat, panting and wet mud. Elephants cool their blood in their ears. Lizards simply move out of the sun.

items.p: Why do frogs lay their eggs in water?
opts: Because frog eggs have no shell and would dry out in air
Because the water keeps them warm
Because frogs cannot walk on land
items.why: Frog eggs are wrapped in jelly, with no shell. In dry air the jelly dries out, as in the Egg in the Air test. Picking 'cannot walk on land' is wrong, because adult frogs hop about on land.

items.p: In the Thar desert, food is hard to find, the days are very hot and the winter nights are freezing. Two friends, Meera and Farida, argue about which kind of animal has the better life there.

views.says: The garden lizard has the better life. They take their heat from the sun, so they need only a few insects a week.
The desert gerbil, a kind of mouse, has the better life. They make their own heat, so they can hunt at night, when it is cool and a lizard is too cold to move.
Both live in the desert, so both ways must work. Look at what each animal gains and what they give up.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give one reason. Then say one thing the other side has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with a reason, such as 'making your own heat burns lots of food, and desert food is scarce.' It also gives the other side fairly: the gerbil can stay busy on a cold night, when the lizard cannot.
items.why: Each way of keeping warm has a cost and a gain. Neither is simply better. A good answer weighs both.

items.p: Which animal feeds their babies milk?
items.why: Mammal mothers feed their babies milk, and a goat is a mammal. Picking hen is common, because hens look after their chicks. But hen chicks peck grain and insects, and drink no milk.

items.p: Look at the chart from the fur coat test. Which bottle kept its warmth best?
items.why: The dry sock bottle cooled only 4 degrees. That is the shortest bar. Picking 'wet sock' means reading the tallest bar as best. Here a tall bar means it lost the most heat.

chart.title: Made-up results from the fur coat test: degrees each bottle cooled in 20 minutes

items.p: Write one way a mammal keeps warm and one way they keep cool.
items.a: For example: a yak keeps warm with thick fur. A dog keeps cool by panting.
items.why: Any correct pair is good. Warm: fur, fat, shivering, huddling. Cool: sweating, panting, mud, shade, flapping ears.

items.p: Why is 'cold-blooded' a confusing word for a lizard?
items.a: Because a lizard's blood is not always cold. In the sun it can be warmer than a person. They just take their heat from outside instead of making it.
items.why: A good answer says the lizard can be warm, and that the real difference is where the heat comes from.

items.p: Draw a fish. Draw arrows to show water going in at the mouth, over the gills and out at the side.
items.a: Arrows go in at the mouth, over the gills behind the eye, and out under the gill flap.
items.why: This shows the path water takes so the gills can take out its oxygen.

items.p: A mudskipper is a fish who hops about on the mud of the Sundarbans at low tide. They have gills, not lungs. How can they breathe out of water?
opts: They keep water in their gill chambers, and take in some oxygen through their wet skin.
They hold their breath for a whole day.
They do not need oxygen on land.
items.why: Gills only work when they are wet. The mudskipper carries a mouthful of water in their gill chambers and keeps their skin damp, rolling in puddles. If they dry out, they cannot breathe. So they never go far from wet mud.

items.p: Why do birds need lots of oxygen?
opts: Flying and making their own heat both use a lot of energy
items.why: Flying and staying warm both burn lots of food, and that needs lots of oxygen. Their lungs with air sacs help.

items.p: A tadpole breathes with gills, but a grown frog breathes with lungs and skin.
items.why: True. As a tadpole changes into a frog, they lose their gills and grow lungs. That is why a frog can live on land but must keep their skin damp.

items.p: A mouse and a snake weigh the same. Which needs more food each week?
items.why: The mouse makes their own heat, which burns many times more food. The snake takes their heat from outside, so they can wait weeks between meals.

items.p: In the Lizard on a Wall test, the sunny tumbler warmed 6 degrees and the shady tumbler warmed 2 degrees. So the sunny one warmed ____ degrees more.
items.why: 6 take away 2 is 4. A lizard on a sunny wall warms up the same way, because they cannot make their own heat. Reading only the tall bar, and saying 6, is a common slip.

items.p: In the fur coat test, why did the wet sock bottle cool fastest?
opts: Wet wool has no trapped air, and drying water carries heat away
items.why: Wet fur or wool loses its trapped air, and the water drying off takes heat with it. That is why a wet dog shivers.

items.p: Put these in order, from the animal that looks after their babies least to most.
items.why: The rohu lays lakhs of eggs and swims away. Sparrow parents warm and feed a few chicks for a few weeks. An elephant mother, with the other females of her herd, cares for one calf for years.

items.p: In olive ridley turtles, warmer nests give more female babies.
items.why: True. In many turtles, the warmth of the sand decides whether a baby is male or female.

items.p: Which animal is a mammal that lays eggs?
items.why: The platypus of Australia is a mammal with fur that feeds their babies milk, but they lay eggs. Picking penguin or crocodile is wrong: they lay eggs but are a bird and a reptile.

items.p: Why does a small bottle of warm water cool faster than a big one?
opts: It has more skin for its size, so heat escapes faster
items.why: A small body has lots of surface for its size, so heat leaks out fast. That is why tiny birds and mice must eat so often.

items.p: Match the animal parent to what they do.
pairs: carries her hatchlings in her mouth
holds the egg on his feet
seals herself in a tree hole with her eggs
items.why: Every group has parents who care for their young, in very different ways.

items.p: Lying in the sun to warm up is called ____.
items.why: Lizards, snakes, crocodiles and turtles bask to warm their bodies.

items.p: A pigeon looks fat and round on a winter morning. Explain why.
items.a: They have fluffed up their feathers. That traps more still air, which keeps their own body heat in.
items.why: A good answer mentions trapped air and keeping heat in.

items.p: Why could the first animals with shelled eggs live further from water than frogs?
items.a: Their eggs did not dry out in air. So they could lay eggs on dry land, away from ponds.
items.why: A good answer links the shell to stopping the egg from drying out.

items.p: Draw a bird's egg, cut in half. Show the shell, the baby, the yolk for food, and the tiny holes that let air in.
items.a: A shell with dots for holes, a small curled chick, a yellow yolk, and clear watery white around them.
items.why: An egg holds what the baby needs: food in the yolk, water in the white, and air that comes in through the shell.

items.p: A lizard on a hot rock is 40 °C. A child in the shade is 37 °C. Which is true?
opts: The lizard makes more heat than the child
The lizard took their heat from the sun, and the child made theirs from food
Thermometers do not work on lizards
items.why: The lizard is warmer, but they took that heat from the sun. The child makes her own. This is why 'cold-blooded' is a misleading word.

items.p: Birds and mammals probably began to make their own heat separately.
items.why: True. Most scientists think birds and mammals came from different groups of ancestors and each became warm on its own. This is still being studied.

items.p: Birds came from dinosaurs. Scientists still argue about how warm the dinosaurs were.

views.says: Some dinosaurs had feathers and grew fast, like birds. So they made their own heat.
The growth rings in dinosaur bones show they were in between. They made some heat, but less than birds or mammals.

views.who: Scientists who study very large animals
views.says: Giant dinosaurs stayed warm just by being huge, like a big pot of water that cools slowly. They did not need to make much heat.

items.ask: Which idea do you find most convincing? Give your reason. Then say what new evidence would change your mind.
items.a: A strong answer uses a piece of evidence, such as feathers, fast-growing bones, or the Big Body, Small Body test where the big bottle cooled more slowly. It says what could change the answer, such as measuring growth rings in many more dinosaur bones. It may say different dinosaurs could have been different.
items.why: This is a real, open argument. A good answer uses evidence and stays ready to change their mind.

items.p: All the warmth of a sparrow comes, in the end, from where?
opts: From the sun, through the grain they eat
items.why: The sparrow burns food to make heat. That food's energy came from plants, which caught it from sunlight. Feathers only hold the heat in.

items.p: A tuna keeps their swimming muscles warmer than the sea. What does this show?
opts: The split between 'makes their own heat' and 'takes heat from outside' is not perfect
items.why: Tuna are fish, but they keep some of their muscles warm. Nature does not always fit our neat groups.

items.p: Put these in the order they first appeared on Earth, oldest first.
items.why: Fish came first, more than 500 million years ago. Some fish gave rise to four-legged animals like amphibians. Then came animals with shelled eggs, the ancestors of reptiles and mammals. Birds came later, from dinosaurs.

items.p: Alligators were found in 2010 to share something with birds. What?
opts: Air flowing one way through their lungs
items.why: Colleen Farmer and Kent Sanders found that air flows one way through alligator lungs, as in birds. Birds and crocodiles are close cousins.

items.p: Kavya, a girl in your class, says: 'My sweater makes heat. That is why I feel warm when I put it on.' What is wrong with her idea? How could the Fur Coat Test show it?
items.a: The sweater makes no heat. It traps still air, which holds in the heat that Kavya's body makes. In the Fur Coat Test, the wrapped bottle still cooled, only more slowly. A sweater on a chair, or wrapped round a bottle of cold water, never gets warm.
items.why: A strong answer says the heat comes from the body, and the wool only slows it leaving. It uses the test as evidence.

items.p: A rohu lays lakhs of eggs. An elephant has one calf every few years. Why might each way work?
items.a: Most rohu eggs are eaten, but there are so many that a few survive. The elephant has one calf, but cares for them for years, so they are very likely to survive.
items.why: A good answer sees the trade: many young with no care, or few young with lots of care.

items.p: Design a fair test to find out whether feathers or cotton wool keep a warm bottle warmer.
items.a: Use two identical bottles with the same warm water. Wrap one in feathers and one in the same amount of cotton wool. Keep them in the same place. Measure both every 5 minutes for 20 minutes.
items.why: A fair test changes only one thing: the wrapping. Everything else stays the same.

items.p: Birds came from dinosaurs, and crocodiles are their closest living cousins. Should birds be called reptiles?

views.who: Scientists who sort animals by their family tree
views.says: Yes. A group should hold an ancestor and all of their children. Birds come from the same family as crocodiles and lizards, so birds are reptiles.

views.who: Scientists who sort animals by their bodies
views.says: No. Birds have feathers, make their own heat and breathe air one way through their lungs. They are so different that they need a group of their own.

items.ask: Which way of sorting do you prefer? Give your reason. Then say why the other way is useful too.
items.a: A strong answer picks a way and gives a reason, then says fairly what the other way does well. For example: the family tree way shows who is related, but the body way helps us talk about birds' feathers and warmth.
items.why: Both are used by real scientists today. The five groups are a tool that people made, not a fact of nature. A good answer sees what each way of sorting is for.

items.p: In 1774, Charles Blagden and George Fordyce sat in a room heated far above the boiling point of water. Eggs left in the room cooked hard. But the two men came out well, dripping with sweat. What does this show?
opts: A body that makes its own heat also works to stay cool, for example by sweating.
People cannot get hot at all.
Eggs cook more easily than people because eggs are smaller.
items.why: Before this, many people thought a body heats up like a stone in the sun. But a living body keeps its own warmth steady. Sweat drying on the skin carries heat away. A stone, or an egg, cannot do that.

items.p: A mother bird sits on her eggs on a cold, windy night. Draw her from the side, cut in half. Label how her body heat reaches the eggs, and what stops the heat escaping.
items.a: The mother's belly touching the eggs, with a bare patch of skin there, labelled 'her heat goes into the eggs'. Fluffed feathers around her and the nest under the eggs, labelled 'trapped still air keeps the heat in'.
items.why: Eggs cannot make their own heat, so the mother lends them hers. Many birds grow a bare 'brood patch' on the belly, so warm skin touches the eggs. Feathers and the nest trap still air, just like the sock in the Fur Coat Test.

items.p: Some snakes, such as Russell's viper, give birth to live babies instead of laying eggs.
items.why: True. The eggs hatch inside the mother, and the babies are born alive.

items.p: Your body makes heat from food all the time, and that heat keeps leaving you. Where does it go? Say what you think.
items.a: Any honest answer. For example: it goes into the air, the chair and my clothes, and then out into the room.
items.why: This is an open question. Good answers give a reason, such as the fur coat test, where heat left even the covered bottle.

opts: An animal that lives in water
quiz.why: Vertebrates are animals with a backbone. Picking 'lives in water' sorts by home, not body. Picking fur describes only mammals.

quiz.p: Which of these is an amphibian?
quiz.why: Frogs have soft, damp skin and lay jelly eggs in water. Lizards and crocodiles have dry scales, so they are reptiles. Mixing them up is very common, because they all have four legs and live near the ground.

quiz.p: A Ganges river dolphin lives in water all their life. How do they breathe?
opts: They come up and breathe air with lungs
quiz.why: Dolphins are mammals. They breathe air with lungs, so they must come up every minute or two. Picking gills means sorting by where an animal lives, not by their body.

quiz.p: Which animal breathes only with gills, all their life?
quiz.why: A rohu has gills from egg to old age. A frog has gills only as a tadpole, then lungs and damp skin. A dolphin has lungs.

quiz.p: All day, a garden lizard moves from a sunny wall into the shade, and back again. Why?
opts: To stay not too cold and not too hot, because they take their heat from outside
To look for food in two places
Because they are scared of the sun
quiz.why: A lizard cannot make or lose heat on purpose the way a sparrow can. So they move: into the sun to warm up, into the shade before they get too hot. Their behaviour does the job that a mammal's or a bird's body does inside.

quiz.p: On a hot day, a dog lies in the shade with their tongue out, panting. How does panting cool the dog?
opts: Water drying off the tongue and mouth carries heat away
quiz.why: When water dries, it takes heat with it. Dogs cannot sweat much through their fur, so they dry water from their tongue instead. Sweat does the same for people.

quiz.p: A yak lives high up in Ladakh, where the winter is freezing. What keeps the yak warm?
opts: Thick, shaggy fur that traps still air, and a layer of fat
quiz.why: The yak makes their own heat from food. The fur holds a layer of still air next to the skin, and fat under the skin slows heat leaving too.

quiz.p: A hen's egg can lie on dry straw for three weeks without drying out. What stops it drying out?
opts: The shell keeps the water in, but tiny holes let air through
The hen sprinkles water on the egg
The yolk soaks up the air
quiz.why: A shelled egg can be laid on land. A frog's jelly egg has no shell, so in dry air it dries out. That is why frogs lay their eggs in water.

quiz.p: What makes mammals different from all other groups?
quiz.why: Mammal mothers make milk in their own bodies to feed their babies. No other group does. Pigeons feed chicks a soft food called crop milk, but it is not real milk. Picking 'lay eggs' is true of most other groups. Picking 'fly' fits bats, but also birds and insects.

quiz.p: In the Fur Coat Test, why did all the bottles start with water at the same warmth?
opts: So that the only difference between them was the coat
quiz.why: In a fair test, you change only one thing. If one bottle started hotter, we could not tell whether the coat or the starting heat made the difference.

quiz.p: What do scientists still argue about?
opts: When animals first began to make their own heat
quiz.why: We know fish have gills and that all birds lay eggs. But nobody is sure when, or why, warm bodies began, or how warm the dinosaurs were.

applications: Doctors use thermometers to check whether a person's steady body warmth has turned into a fever.
Warm clothes, quilts and sleeping bags copy fur and feathers by trapping still air.
Thermos flasks and cool boxes slow heat moving in or out, like fur and feathers.
Poultry farmers use incubators to keep eggs at the warmth a hen would give them.
Fish farmers pump air into ponds, so the fish have enough oxygen for their gills.
Zoos give reptiles warm lamps and basking stones, because they take their heat from outside.
Wet khus curtains cool a room the way wet mud cools a buffalo: the water dries and carries heat away.
Wildlife rescuers keep fallen baby birds warm, and try to return them to their nests.

open_questions.q: When did animals first start making their own body heat, and why?
open_questions.why_open: Body heat does not leave clear marks in fossils. Scientists use clues from bones, nose bones and growth rings, and they disagree.

open_questions.q: How will a warming world change turtles, whose nest warmth decides if babies are male or female?
open_questions.why_open: Turtles may change when and where they nest. Scientists are watching beaches around the world to find out.

open_questions.q: How many kinds of frogs live in India that nobody has found yet?
open_questions.why_open: New frogs are still being discovered in the Western Ghats and the north-east almost every year.

open_questions.q: Do fish feel the cold the way we do?
open_questions.why_open: Fish can sense temperature and swim to warmer or cooler water. But what it feels like to them, nobody knows.

maths.problem: In the fur coat test, the bare bottle started at 48 °C and ended at 42 °C. The dry sock bottle started at 48 °C and ended at 44 °C. How many degrees did each one cool? How many more degrees did the bare bottle cool?
maths.answer: The bare bottle cooled 6 degrees. The sock bottle cooled 4 degrees. The bare bottle cooled 2 degrees more.
maths.explain: Bare bottle: 48 take away 42 is 6. Sock bottle: 48 take away 44 is 4. Then 6 take away 4 is 2. So without its coat, the bottle lost 2 more degrees of warmth.
maths.context: This is about the fur coat test. Three bottles of warm water stood in for animals. One had no coat and one had a dry woollen sock. You measured how warm they were with a thermometer.
maths.why_maths: Taking the last reading from the first tells us how much warmth each bottle lost. Then we can say exactly how much the coat helped.

maths.problem: In the lizard on a wall test, the sunny tumbler warmed from 26 °C to 32 °C in 30 minutes. About how many degrees did it warm every 10 minutes, if it warmed evenly?
maths.explain: 32 take away 26 is 6 degrees in 30 minutes. 30 minutes is 3 lots of 10 minutes. 6 divided by 3 is 2. So about 2 degrees every 10 minutes.
maths.context: This is about the lizard on a wall test. A tumbler of cool water was put in the sun, like a basking lizard, and measured with a thermometer.
maths.why_maths: Sharing the warming out over time tells us how long a lizard might need to bask before they are warm enough to hunt.

maths.problem: Your body temperature was 36.8 °C in the morning and 37.1 °C in the evening. The air was 18 °C in the morning and 27 °C in the evening. How much did each change?
maths.answer: The air changed by 9 degrees. Your body changed by only 0.3 of a degree, less than one degree.
maths.explain: Air: 27 take away 18 is 9. Body: 37.1 take away 36.8 is 0.3. Think of it as 371 tenths take away 368 tenths, which is 3 tenths. So the air changed a lot and your body hardly changed.
maths.context: This is about the three-day body temperature diary. You measured the air and your own body in the morning and the evening.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the two changes shows, with numbers, that a body that makes its own heat stays steady while the world changes.

maths.problem: An olive ridley turtle lays about 100 eggs in one nest. If only 1 in every 10 hatchlings survives their first year, how many from one nest survive? If a sparrow lays 4 eggs and 2 chicks survive, which parent has more surviving young from one nest?
maths.answer: About 10 turtles survive. 2 sparrows survive. The turtle has more survivors, even though she gives no care.
maths.explain: 100 divided into groups of 10 gives 10 groups. One survivor from each group is 10 turtles. The sparrow has 2. So laying many eggs can work, even with no care.
maths.context: This is about the chart you made in 'Who looks after the babies?'. It compared how many eggs animals lay and how much they care for them. The survival numbers here are made up to keep the sums simple.

roots.context: We have been learning how fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals breathe, keep warm and have young. Now we ask what their warmth tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: In the fur coat test, even the bottle in the dry sock kept cooling. A sparrow loses heat like that every minute, and makes new heat from food to replace it. A lizard lets their body cool at night and warms up again in the sun. That is why a sparrow must eat many times more than a lizard of the same weight.
deep_truth.habit: We say a sparrow 'is warm-blooded', as if their warmth were fixed, like the colour of their feathers. In fact their heat leaks away all the time, and has to be made again from food.
deep_truth.evidence: In the fur coat test, every bottle cooled, even the one in the dry sock. In the body diary, your temperature stayed near 37 °C while the air changed by many degrees. A mouse needs many times more food than a snake of the same weight, because they keep making heat.

three.who_am_i: You are a body that stays near 37 degrees, because you make new heat from food every minute, even while you sleep.
three.what_is_life: Staying alive and warm means never stopping: eating, breathing and making heat, day and night.
three.what_is_this_world: A world where a lizard is about as warm as the air around them, and a pigeon keeps their own warmth with food and feathers.

roots.thread: All animals with a backbone come from early fish that lived in the sea more than 500 million years ago. From that one beginning came frogs, crocodiles, sparrows, cows and you. Each group found its own way to breathe, keep warm and have young. They still share one body plan, a backbone with a skull at one end. And the warmth of every one of them comes, in the end, from the same sun.

science.text: Nearly all the energy that warms and moves animals on Earth comes from sunlight, caught first by plants and other green living things. A few living communities, around hot springs deep in the sea, run on chemical energy from the Earth instead.
Every body that is warmer than its surroundings is always losing heat to them. Fur, feathers and fat only slow this down.

practice.title: Holding warmth
practice.say: Let's sit quietly. Cup your hands together in front of your mouth. Breathe out slowly into them, three times. Feel the warmth of your breath in your hands. Now open your hands a little, and feel the warmth slip away into the room. Sit still for a moment. Your warmth is going out into the air, where the lizard, the bird and the trees are. Where did that warmth come from this morning? Where is it going now?
practice.kid: Cup your hands. Breathe out into them three times. Feel the warmth. Open your hands. Feel it float away.

how_we_found_out.story: About 300 years ago, the Dutch doctor Herman Boerhaave put small animals in very hot rooms, and they died. Many people then believed that no animal could live in air hotter than their own body. They thought a body would simply heat up like a stone left in the sun. In 1774, the English doctor Charles Blagden decided to test this on himself. With his friend George Fordyce, he sat in a small room heated far above the boiling point of water. They took a dog with them, in a basket so their feet would not burn. Eggs left in the room cooked hard. But the men and the dog came out well, and their bodies had stayed close to their usual warmth. Blagden saw that they were dripping with sweat. He suggested that sweat drying on the skin carries heat away. A living body keeps working to hold its own temperature, in the cold and in the heat.
how_we_found_out.who: Charles Blagden and George Fordyce, with the earlier idea from Herman Boerhaave
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That no animal can live in air hotter than their own body, because a body heats up like any other object.
